 "Ghost students" stole millions in federal aid until data patterns gave them away
 Data analysis flagged the fraud, and the FBI traced the money to bank accounts and crypto wallets
 By Skye Jacobs 
 November 1, 2026, 11:37 
 10 comments 
 Add TechSpot 
 Serving tech enthusiasts for over 25 years.
 TechSpot means tech analysis and advice you can trust .
 Connecting the dots: Federal prosecutors in Nebraska, Virginia and New Jersey have charged five people in a student aid fraud scheme that used AI to fake coursework and class attendance. The case also led to a cryptocurrency seizure in Kenya. It shows how AI is making fake students harder to spot, just as the automated identity checks meant to stop them raise new concerns about real students being wrongly flagged. 
 Unusual patterns in federal student aid data led the Justice Department to charge five people and seize more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency tied to a network associated with Kenyan nationals. The charges are the first results of a broader federal effort, which the department calls Operation Ghostbusters, to crack down on "ghost student" fraud.
 The scheme used stolen identities to enroll fake students in colleges, and relied partly on AI to keep those students looking active long enough to collect aid.
 The case began at the Department of Education's Office of Inspector General, which first spotted the fraud patterns. The FBI then worked out how many accounts were involved and followed the money into US and foreign bank accounts and crypto wallets.
 Theophani K. Stamos, First Assistant US Attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, said at a press conference that data analysis "identified unusual, suspicious patterns of behavior." The FBI said those patterns showed coordinated fraud involving the FAFSA, which Stamos said gave investigators "a solid basis and a solid lead to open further inquiries that have led to indictments."
 Some of the money trails were large. One defendant used accounts at several financial institutions to receive more than 700 fraudulent aid refund deposits worth about $1.44 million, the Justice Department said. Inside Higher Ed reported that another person received more than $1 million in deposits linked to more than 300 fake student accounts.

 The FBI has identified more than $32 million in losses from similar ghost student schemes, officials said, and believes the true total is "substantially higher."
 The wider exposure may be far bigger. The Education Department has "identified over 830,000 potentially fraudulent federal student aid accounts created by using this PII of US citizens," officials said. If every one of those accounts turns out to be a ghost student, the Justice Department estimates losses close to $130 million. Stamos's office has sent "approximately 50 referrals to 26 FBI field offices across the country."
 The scheme starts with purchased personal data. The usual targets are people who finished high school and went straight to work. Because they have no college record, the Education Department has nothing to cross-check the applications against. The fraudsters file FAFSA forms and apply to universities and community colleges.
 If a fake student is accepted, the aid goes first to the school for tuition and fees, and whatever is left is sent to bank accounts the fraudsters control. Dozens of Americans have opened accounts to serve as money mules, the Justice Department said.
 AI helps keep the fake students from being detected. It fills out applications, completes coursework and, in some cases, creates the appearance of a person attending online classes.
 "It looks like the ghost student is actually completing the class," said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division. "Some even create the appearance of a fake student in an online classroom to trick schools into believing a real person is present. The goal is to keep the ghost student in school for as long as possible, semester after semester after semester."
 The Justice Department believes the scheme has been running since at least 2021 and has grown more sophisticated as AI has opened new ways to steal loans. McDonald credited fraud-detection measures introduced by the Trump administration for the arrests and called the Kenyan seizure "the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya."
 Victims often find out only years later, when the government tries to collect on the loans. By then their credit may already be damaged. "The Department of Education does a great job to help unravel that mess, but it is a mess that no one should have to endure," McDonald said.
 Under identity verification rules the Education Department added this year, applicants hold a government-issued ID up to their camera in real time while automated systems review it. A senior department official told Inside Higher Ed the systems are "similar to the ones used by financial services companies like banks." Each applicant then gets a risk rating, and anyone rated "high risk" is rejected.
 After that, it is up to the school to check whether the application was real. Federal Trade Commission Chairman Andrew Ferguson, vice chair of the White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, argued that this kind of automation can stop fraud without adding staff. "The computers help us find it, and we keep the money in the agency," he said.
 The software has already had problems. In August, the department confirmed that a technical issue from June 29 to July 6 kept fraud evaluation results from being attached to certain FAFSA forms. Those applications were later reprocessed. Advocates also warn that false flags put more work on schools and can delay aid. MorraLee Keller, a senior consultant for the National College Attainment Network, told Inside Higher Ed that "a lot of low-economic kids may not have secured, for example, a driver's license." Students who correct their FAFSA can also be screened again, which means a false rejection could hold up their money.
 The administration says it expects few real students to be flagged, but it hasn't put a number on it. In April, Melanie Storey, president of the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators, asked the department on an association podcast "to quantify the volume of in-person verification that will remain." Aaron Lemon-Strauss, executive director of the FAFSA program, replied, "I'm not going to be able to give you a number yet." For students who "accidentally get caught in the net," he urged universities to stay vigilant.
